The Biotechnology Innovation Organization (BIO) appreciates the opportunity to comment

BIO is the premier biotechnology advocacy organization representing biotech

some of the worldâ€™s largest biopharmaceutical companies, all united by the  
same goal -- to develop medical and scientific breakthroughs that prevent and fight  
disease, restore health, and improve patientsâ€™ lives. BIO also organizes the BIO

investment, and progress within the sector. 
 
A central part of our mission is to ensure that patients can access clinically appropriate 
prescription medicines in a timely manner, as prescribed by their provider.  
 
 
Summary of BIOâ€™s Comments 
 
BIOâ€™s comments on CMS-0062-P are guided by the following overarching principles.
2 
 
â€¢ 
Interoperability is a valuable tool that can improve patient care when it is designed 
and implemented in a patient-centered manner. 
 
â€¢ 
Inappropriate prior authorization and step therapy continue to delay, disrupt, and in 
some cases prevent access to medically necessary prescription medicines. 
 
â€¢ 
BIO applauds expanding electronic prior authorization to drugs covered under 
medical and pharmacy benefits. BIO appreciates that doing so can shorten prior 
authorization timelines, enabling patients to receive care faster. However, CMS 
should ensure that these requirements, designed to speed the prior authorization 
process, do not expand inappropriate utilization management. 
 
â€¢ 
CMS should pair interoperability requirements with greater data collection regarding 
utilization management.  
 
 
Interoperability Standards for APIs (Section II.A, Page 19900) 
 
In the proposed rule, CMS proposes to strengthen and standardize the technical framework 
underlying interoperability-enabling application programming interfaces (APIs). CMS 
proposes changes designed to tighten interoperability standards, formalize Fast Healthcare 
Interoperability Resources (FHIR)-based transactions, and ensure more uniform technical 
implementation across impacted payers. 
 
CMS is proposing to adopt FHIR as a HIPAA transaction standard for the first time, elevating 
FHIR from an implementation choice to a regulatory requirement. The rule also converts 
several previously optional technical implementation guides into mandatory standards, 
therefore increasing consistency across plans. Notably, CMS proposes an October 1, 2027, 
compliance deadline for the new requirements (HIPAA transaction-standard proposals would 
follow a separate compliance timeline tied to finalization of the rule).  
 
BIO Comment: BIO agrees that a more standardized electronic exchange of 
information can reduce administrative burdens, improve care coordination, and 
enhance the overall quality of care patients receive across the United States. In 
particular, thoughtful use of APIs and other standards to expedite and streamline the 
prior authorization process has the potential to reduce unnecessary friction for 
patients, providers, and health plans alike. BIO appreciates that the proposed rule 
extends many of these standards to prescription drugs. 
 
Nevertheless, BIO remains deeply concerned that utilization management practices, 
especially prior authorization and step therapy, continue to be a significant barrier to 
timely access to care. Without intentional and thoughtful guardrails, 
technology-enabled prior authorization risks make existing access to care barriers 
more pernicious rather than alleviating them. BIO believes the proposals in this rule 
alone will not fully address the core of the problem impacting patient access to care. 
 
Despite recent advances in health information technology, utilization management 
remains a central driver of delayed or abandoned patient care. A Kaiser Family 
Foundation (KFF) poll conducted earlier this year found that prior authorization ranks 
3 
as the â€œpublicâ€™s biggest burden when getting healthcare.â€1 Patients frequently face 
delays, even when therapies are supported by established clinical guidelines and 
standards of care. These harms especially impact patients with rare diseases when 
new therapies emerge.2 In these cases, time is often critical, and repeated utilization 
management barriers can disrupt the chances of meaningful clinical benefit. In fact, 
one-third of doctors have witnessed excessive prior authorizations and untimely 
decisions lead to â€œserious adverse eventsâ€ for patients.3 
 
Evidence from physician surveys, patient access analyses, and payer utilization data 
consistently demonstrates that prior authorization delays for prescription medicines 
are associated with treatment abandonment, worsening symptoms, and avoidable 
complications. In a survey of practicing physicians, 93% of physicians reported that 
prior authorizations caused patient care delays, and 82% shared that it can lead to 
treatment abandonment.4 
 
Delays in initiating or continuing therapy can lead to disease progression and 
increased use of emergency and inpatient services, even after a health plan agrees 
to pay for a treatment.5 For patients with conditions such as cancer, autoimmune 
disease, rare genetic disorders, or other serious illnesses, interruptions in therapy 
can have irreversible consequences for long-term outcomes and quality of life.6  
 
Furthermore, sophisticated knowledge of the United States healthcare system is 
often necessary for navigating a prior authorization denial. Within Medicare 
Advantage specifically, 80.7% of prior authorization denials were eventually 
overturned on appeal â€“ though frequently only after significant delay, according to 
KFF.7 While on the one hand, it may be encouraging that patients eventually received 
the care they were prescribed, on the other hand, the high successful appeal rate 
suggests dubious clinical grounds for application of prior authorizations in the first 
place. These excessive and unnecessary prior authorization rates are concerning and 
pose unnecessary delays in care and significant health risks to patients. 
 
Despite the high rate of overturn on appeal, only 11.5% of MA prior authorizations 
were appealed at all.8 This, at least in part, showcases a larger problem: only those 
with in-depth knowledge of the healthcare system are aware that appealing a prior 
authorization decision is even an option. Prior authorization and the complexity and 
opacity associated with it are harming patient care.

BIO urges CMS to make prior authorization appeals straightforward and patient

standards are an important first step toward improving utilization management 
processes. While standardization alone will not resolve inappropriate utilization 
management, it can create the platform for meaningful process improvement and 
accountability. As data builds year over year, CMS may consider whether prior 
authorizations or step edits are necessary for a particular service or drug, much as

Electronic Prior Authorization for Drugs (Section II.B, Page 19921) 
 
The proposed rule would expand electronic prior authorization requirements finalized under 
the 2024 Interoperability and Prior Authorization final rule to now include drugs.9  
 
For drugs covered under a medical benefit, CMS proposes to require impacted payers to 
incorporate these drugs into the Prior Authorization API framework established under the 
2024 final rule. This would apply the same electronic prior authorization workflow used for 
non-drug items and services, including coverage requirements discovery, documentation 
templates, prior authorization submission, and payer responses to drugs. The proposed 
compliance date for medical benefit drug prior authorization requirements is October 1, 
2027, following the January 1, 2027, compliance date for non-drug prior authorization 
requirements finalized in the 2024 rule.  
 
For drugs covered under a pharmacy benefit, CMS proposes to require non-Medicare 
impacted payers to support three National Council for Prescription Drug Programs 
standards: SCRIPT, Formulary and Benefit, and Real-Time Prescription Benefit. These 
standards support electronic prior authorization, formulary inquiries, and real-time benefit 
checks and are already required for Medicare Part D plans. The proposal would extend 
similar requirements to non-Medicare payers, including Medicaid and CHIP fee-for-service 
programs, Medicaid and CHIP managed care plans, and Qualified Health Plans offered on the 
federally facilitated Exchange. 
 
CMS also notes that, outside of Medicare, there is no existing regulatory definition 
distinguishing drugs covered under a medical benefit from those covered under a pharmacy 
benefit. For non-Medicare impacted payers, CMS would require plans to assess their covered 
drugs and determine, on a drug-by-drug basis, which electronic prior authorization pathway 
applies. 
 
BIO Comment: BIO supports CMSâ€™s proposal to require electronic prior 
authorization capabilities for prescription drugs, including drugs covered under both 
medical and pharmacy benefits.  
 
 
9 https://www.cms.gov/newsroom/fact-sheets/cms-interoperability-prior-authorization-final-
rule-cms-0057-f 
5 
BIO believes a lack of standardization has contributed to fragmented prior 
authorization workflows that burden providers and can leave patients without 
life-saving medication. Manual processes, duplicative documentation requests, a lack 
of a uniform prior authorization form, and inconsistent coverage rules frequently 
delay care unnecessarily. These challenges are particularly significant for prescription 
drugs, which are increasingly subject to prior authorization across payer types and 
benefit structures. 
 
Patients often require therapies administered in different settings and under different 
benefit structures, and inconsistent workflows can exacerbate delays and confusion 
for both patients and providers. When implemented appropriately, such as to assure 
patient safety based on drug labelling for certain conditions or to avoid problematic 
drug-drug interactions, electronic prior authorization can help ensure that providers 
understand coverage requirements upfront, submit complete information once, and 
receive timely determinations. For patients, this can reduce uncertainty and stress at 
moments when medical needs are urgent. 
 
However, BIO urges CMS to ensure that electronic prior authorization requirements 
do not result unnecessarily in more frequent or more complex utilization 
management applications. The decision to subject a drug to prior authorization 
should be driven by clinical appropriateness and patient need. However, faster 
denials or more efficient requests for additional documentation do not constitute 
meaningful reform from a patient perspective. To ensure that electronic prior 
authorization is not used as a barrier to care, it must be limited to cases where it is 
clinically appropriate--electronic prior authorization cannot be a substitute for 
clinically appropriate decision making. 
 
BIO additionally encourages CMS to consider how electronic prior authorization for 
drugs interacts with real-world provider workflows. Providers and their staff report 
spending 13 hours per week completing prior authorization requests, diverting time 
and resources away from direct patient care.10 One way to help alleviate this burden 
would be for CMS to establish a standardized prior authorization framework that all 
impacted payers must accept. 
 
Today, health plans rely on varied forms, requirements, and clinical criteria for 
submitting prior authorization requests. This requires providers to navigate different 
data fields and processes for each payer. Rather than relying on payer-specific 
formats, CMSâ€™s proposals would improve efficiency by requiring a common set of 
data elements, fields, and clinical questions that can be submitted electronically 
across plans. Because many prior authorization requests are resolved on the first 
submission based on basic coverage and clinical information, a standardized 
approach would streamline these routine transactions and reduce duplicative data 
entry while improving interoperability across systems. Aligning prior authorization 
requirements in this manner would help ensure that electronic solutions reduce 
administrative burden and integrate more effectively into clinical workflows. BIO 
believes that this strategy will improve patient experience and help ensure that 
patients receive medically recommended care in a timely manner with minimal 
administrative friction.  
 
 
10 https://www.ama-assn.org/system/files/prior-authorization-survey.pdf 
6 
BIO also encourages CMS to protect continuity of care when patients switch coverage 
by requiring payers to honor previous prior authorization approvals for prescription 
drugs. The interoperability infrastructure contemplated by this rule should make it 
easier for plans to recognize existing approvals and avoid unnecessarily requiring 
patients and providers to restart utilization management processes that have already 
been completed. 
 
In response to CMSâ€™s proposal to require non-Medicare-impacted payers to assess 
covered drugs and determine, on a drug-by-drug basis, which electronic prior 
authorization pathway applies, BIO recommends that CMS clarify how it will monitor 
and evaluate these plan determinations. Without clear oversight or operational 
expectations, this flexibility could lead to avoidable delays or confusion for providers 
navigating the electronic prior authorization process. CMS should consider guardrails 
or reporting mechanisms to promote transparency and consistency, including an 
expectation that plans redirect electronic prior authorization requests to the 
appropriate pathway when they are initially submitted through the incorrect channel, 
assuming all required information is provided. 
 
This includes considering guardrails or reporting mechanisms to promote 
transparency, consistency, and accountability in how plans assign drugs to specific 
prior authorization pathways. 
 
Lastly, BIO recommends that CMS require plans to update their formulary and prior 
authorization requirements to API portals as close to real-time as possible to capture 
mid-year changes to ensure that patients and providers have up-to-date information. 
This aligns with CMSâ€™s broader position on ensuring patients have timely access to 
information related to their care.   
 
 
Improving Communications and Decision Timeframes for Prior Authorizations 
(Section II.C, Page 19932) 
 
CMS proposes to update and standardize prior authorization decision timeframes for drugs 
across Medicare Advantage, Medicaid, CHIP, and Qualified Health Plan issuers on the 
federally facilitated Exchanges. This builds on prior authorization requirements previously 
finalized for non-drug items and services and addresses gaps in existing drug-specific rules. 
 
Medicare Advantage 
CMS proposes to require Medicare Advantage plans to issue prior authorization decisions for 
drugs within 24 hours for urgent requests and 72 hours for standard requests. 
 
Qualified Health Plan Issuers on the Federally Facilitated Exchanges 
For Qualified Health Plan issuers on the federally facilitated Exchanges, CMS proposes new 
requirements, effective October 1, 2027, to notify requesting providers of prior 
authorization decisions for drugs within 72 hours for standard requests and 24 hours for 
expedited requests. While existing regulations establish patient notification timelines, CMS 
notes there is currently no requirement for Qualified Health Plan issuers to notify providers 
within defined timeframes and proposes to establish that obligation.  
 
Medicaid and CHIP 
CMS proposes to address gaps in prior authorization decision timeframes for drugs under 
Medicaid and CHIP, particularly for drugs that are not classified as â€œcovered outpatient 
drugsâ€ under section 1927 of the Social Security Act. For drugs provided as part of, or 
7 
incident to, bundled services, such as inpatient hospital services, CMS proposes to apply the 
same prior authorization decision timeframes used for non-drug items and services (7 days 
for standard requests; 72 hours for expedited requests). CMS also seeks comment on 
whether additional drug categories should instead be subject to the 24-hour statutory 
timeframe applicable to covered outpatient drugs. For state CHIP fee-for-service programs, 
CMS further proposes to shorten prior authorization decision timeframes for prescription 
drugs to no later than 24 hours, aligning them with Medicaid drug prior authorization 
requirements. 
 
Denial Communications 
Across Medicaid and CHIP fee-for-service programs, Medicaid managed care plans, CHIP 
managed care entities, and Qualified Health Plan issuers on the federally facilitated 
Exchanges, CMS proposes to require payers to provide a specific reason to providers when 
denying a prior authorization request for drugs, regardless of the method used to submit or 
communicate the prior authorization request or decision. 
 
BIO Comment: BIO supports CMSâ€™s efforts to establish new prior authorization 
maximum response times and to improve communication and establish clearer 
expectations surrounding prior authorization decision timeframes. 
 
BIO notes, however, that formal timelines alone are insufficient if payers routinely 
rely on repeated requests for additional information, resubmissions, or appeals to 
extend the authorization process. Evidence shows that patients who encounter 
repeated denials or prolonged approval processes frequently fail to initiate 
subsequent therapy, even when clinically appropriate alternatives exist.11 
 
Relatedly, mirroring the policy from the 2024 Prior Authorization Final Rule for 
non-drug items and services, BIO supports CMSâ€™s proposal to require state Medicaid 
and CHIP fee-for-service programs, Medicaid managed care plans, CHIP managed 
care entities, and Qualified Health Plan issuers on the federally facilitated Exchanges 
to provide a specific reason for prior authorization denials for drugs. This 
requirement is essential to ensure that denials are meaningful and actionable for 
providers and patients. 
 
In addition, if AI-based tools are used to make any denials or adverse 
determinations within the prior authorization process, CMS should require a qualified 
clinician to review and sign off on those decisions within standard decision 
timeframes to ensure timely access to care. In addition, patients, prescribers, and 
providers should be informed when AI contributes to a decision and receive a clear, 
understandable explanation of the rationale. Greater transparency is needed so that 
patients and providers understand how determinations are made and whether 
automated tools were involved in a denial or request for additional information. CMS 
should also ensure that any data used by AI-based tools in the prior authorization 
process is up-to-date, complete, and clinically appropriate. When used, AI-enabled 
systems should exclusively support sound clinical decision-making. 
 
For Medicaid-covered outpatient drugs, BIO also supports CMSâ€™s proposal to align 
prior authorization decision timeframes with the statutory requirements governing 
covered outpatient drugs under Section 1927 of the Social Security Act across the 
 
11 https://www.iqvia.com/-/media/iqvia/pdfs/us/white-paper/2025/iqvia-payer-controls-in-
part-d-white-paper-2025.pdf 
8 
board. Applying extended or discretionary timelines to statutorily covered drugs 
undermines congressional intent and delays access to necessary care. 
 
In Medicare Advantage, BIO appreciates CMSâ€™s proposal to require plans to issue 
prior authorization decisions for drugs within 24 hours for urgent requests and within 
72 hours for standard requests. Nevertheless, BIO encourages CMS to further 
consider adopting a 24-hour timeline for both urgent and non-urgent requests to 
ensure that the electronic prior authorization infrastructure required under the rule is 
fully leveraged to facilitate timely access to care. A uniform 24-hour timeline 
requirement should be paired with CMS oversight, along with research and data 
collection, to ensure compressed timelines do not inadvertently lead to plans issuing 
expedited, clinically inappropriate denials in aid of clearing potential backlogs, rather 
than conducting substantive reviews. 
 
Across all impacted payers, BIO recommends that CMS require denials to be 
automatically reviewed by a specialist with expertise in the patientâ€™s specific 
diagnosis. This will help ensure that denials are not made in error and are clinically 
appropriate.    
 
Finally, BIO encourages CMS to closely follow the effect of these proposed rules after 
their implementation to ensure that electronic prior authorization, coupled with 
defined decision timeframes, meaningfully improves real-world access to life-saving 
prescription medicines. 
 
 
Prior Authorization Metrics and Reporting for Drugs (Sections II.C.7 and II.F, 
Pages 19941 and 19969) 
 
CMS proposes to expand its prior authorization transparency framework by requiring 
impacted payers to publicly report detailed prior authorization metrics for drugs and by 
incorporating drug-related prior authorization information into existing interoperability APIs.  
 
Under the proposal, MA organizations, state Medicaid and CHIP fee-for-service programs, 
Medicaid and CHIP managed care entities, and Qualified Health Plans issuers on the 
federally facilitated Exchanges would be required to annually post drug prior authorization 
metrics on their public websites beginning in 2028, using data from the 2027 reporting 
period. Metrics would include approval and denial rates, outcomes following appeal, 
decision-time averages and medians, and data on requests subject to extended review 
timeframes. CMS proposes to require not only percentages but also the underlying 
numerators and denominators, which would allow for a more complete interpretation of the 
data. 
 
Notably, while Part D drugs would be excluded from the scope due to existing reporting 
requirements, Medicare Advantage reporting would generally focus on Part B drugs (with 
CMS requesting comment on whether certain Part A drugs should also be included) 
 
CMS also proposes to modify reporting timelines and aggregation levels for Medicaid and 
CHIP managed care plans by shifting the reporting deadline from a fixed March 31 date to 
90 days after the end of each planâ€™s rating period and requiring reporting at both the plan 
and program level.  
 
9 
BIO Comment: BIO applauds CMSâ€™s interest in collecting and reporting data on 
prior authorization processes. Thoughtfully designed metrics and a robust feedback 
loop of data can help identify patterns of delay, inappropriate denials, or excessive 
utilization management. 
 
BIO supports CMSâ€™s proposal to add new non-drug metrics (such as counts 
underlying existing percentages, denials after appeal, and extended-timeframe 
outcomes) as public reporting requirements and appreciates the quick 
implementation. This will ensure CMS has sufficient data to better oversee utilization 
management programs. 
 
However, BIO does not believe that annual reporting of prior authorization metrics 
for drugs is sufficient. BIO recommends that CMS retain the authority to require 
more frequent reporting where warranted. Specifically, CMS should be able to trigger 
additional reporting if annual data indicate: (1) access concerns for enrollees relative 
to other plans, or (2) prior authorization utilization that materially exceeds central 
tendency benchmarks. This approach would provide CMS with more timely visibility 
into payer practices and better inform future rulemaking. 
 
BIO also supports CMSâ€™s proposal to shift the reporting deadline for Medicaid and 
CHIP managed care plans from March 31 to 90 days after the end of each contract 
rating period and to require reporting at both the plan and program level. In 
addition, BIO recommends that plans should report at the therapeutic area level for 
drugs, to ensure patients with specific conditions are not experiencing access 
problems. These changes promote transparency and accountability and will help 
patients in the long run. 
 
At the same time, BIO cautions that prior authorization metrics must be interpreted 
carefully and in context. Approval rates alone do not capture patient impact, nor do 
they reflect whether utilization management practices align with clinical evidence. As 
a result, CMS should consider adding data on repeated denials, appeal reversals, and 
extended delays to the list of metrics collected.  
 
When finalizing the rule, CMS should ensure that reporting requirements support 
accountability and quality improvement without incentivizing restrictive utilization 
management practices that harm patient access. Ensuring that reporting 
requirements drive meaningful insight and improvement, rather than process-driven 
behavior which could restrict access or distort care decisions, is critical to achieving 
the goals of this rulemaking. 
 
 
Modifications to HIPAA Standards Related to Prior Authorization (Section II.H.11, 
Page 19998) 
 
CMS explains that the existing HIPAA electronic transaction standards include an exception 
for â€œdirect data entryâ€ (DDE), which allows providers to submit information through payer 
portals without using standardized formats. CMS notes that this exception has contributed 
to continued reliance on partially electronic prior authorization processes, such as web 
portals, which remain widely used and are more burdensome and less efficient than fully 
electronic, standards-based transactions. Advances in interoperability standards now enable 
faster, more automated prior authorization workflows with less manual data entry and fewer 
errors. While CMS does not propose changes to the DDE exception in this rule, the Agency 
seeks stakeholder input on whether and how the exception should be updated or narrowed 
10 
in future rulemaking, given its continued impact on the adoption of fully electronic prior 
authorization transactions. 
 
BIO Comment: BIO encourages CMS to narrow the direct data entry exception over 
time. Health plan web portals may remain useful as a limited fallback, but they 
should not serve as a permanent substitute for standards-based electronic prior 
authorization transactions. This is essential, as the portal exception will limit 
electronic prior authorization transactions until it is modified. 
 
 
Response to CMS Request for Information: Step Therapy (Section III.D.2, Page 
20013) 
 
BIO appreciates CMSâ€™s request for information regarding step therapy and welcomes the 
opportunity to comment, specifically on how technology may facilitate step therapy 
determinations in addition to improving the process for step therapy issued by a previous 
payer. 
 
BIO Comment: In general, BIO supports the Agencyâ€™s efforts and agrees that 
improved interoperability across payers could meaningfully improve the transparency 
and administration of step therapy. Specifically, BIO appreciates CMSâ€™s proposal to 
allow patients to avoid having to repeat step therapy protocols already completed 
with a prior payer. 
 
However, this will only be effective alongside increased transparency surrounding 
step therapy at a high level. Merely sending denial decisions regarding step therapy 
to patients faster will not address many of the root problems with this often 
problematic utilization management tool. 
 
Although framed in technical, rather than policy terms, BIO nevertheless views the 
Step Therapy RFI as a critical opportunity to assess the real-world impacts of step 
therapy on patients and to re-examine the Medicare Advantage Part B drug step 
therapy policy implemented in 2019, which BIO believes is harmful to patients and 
should be rescinded.12 
 
BIO believes a number of steps would improve the care patients receive when 
undergoing step therapy treatment: 
 
â€¢ 
Rescind the Medicare Advantage Part B Drug Step Therapy Policy. 
 
â€¢ 
Take further action to ensure step therapy does not impede timely access to 
clinically appropriate care, particularly for patients with serious and life-
threatening conditions and who are stable on current therapies.  
 
â€¢ 
Create guardrails to ensure that any use of step therapy aligns with evidence-
based clinical guidelines, respects physician judgment, and prioritizes patient 
health over other considerations. 
 
 
12 https://www.cms.gov/medicare/health-
plans/healthplansgeninfo/downloads/ma_step_therapy_hpms_memo_8_7_2018.pdf 
11 
â€¢ 
Establish clear, actionable, and timely exceptions to step therapy protocols to 
prevent patient harm, including when treatments are ineffective, 
contraindicated, or when the patient is stable on an existing therapy. 
 
â€¢ 
Collect data evaluating the frequency with which patients do not follow 
through with their care after being subject to step therapy. 
 
â€¢ 
Assess the extent to which step therapy contributes to treatment delays, 
disease progression, and downstream utilization, including emergency 
department visits and hospitalizations. 
 
â€¢ 
Improve data transparency and public visibility around step therapy practices.  
 
â€¢ 
Improve transparency around step therapy protocols, including greater public 
accessibility of utilization management criteria. 
 
â€¢ 
Advocate for improved tracking of step therapy through claims data and 
reporting, including clearer and more public reporting on how often 
therapeutic areas are subject to step therapy. 
 
â€¢ 
Define a standardized set of data elements and a consistent framework for 
tracking step therapy activity to support interoperability, transparency, and 
consistent reporting across payers. 
 
â€¢ 
Use step therapy data collection to inform future CMS rulemaking, recognizing 
that better data is essential to assessing whether step therapy improves care 
or causes harm. 
 
â€¢ 
Ensure that step therapy requirements do not disrupt continuity of care when 
patients change health plans. 
 
â€¢ 
Leverage the payer-to-payer API finalized in the 2024 interoperability rule to 
ensure that patients transitioning between plans are not required to repeat 
step therapy requirements that have already been met. 
 
â€¢ 
Ensure that step therapy determinations and exceptions follow the patient 
across plan transitions to support continuity of care and reduce duplicative 
utilization management requirements. 
 
â€¢ 
Implement step therapy reforms as quickly as possible, recognizing that 
delays in implementing policy changes directly translate into delays in patient 
access to care. 
 
Impact of Step Therapy on Patient Access and Outcomes 
 
While step therapy is sometimes described as a cost-containment or 
care-management tool, real-world evidence demonstrates that it frequently delays 
access to clinically appropriate therapy, interferes with physician decision making, 
12 
and worsens patient outcomes.13,14 Step therapy requirements do not always align 
with established clinical guidelines and standards of care. This is particularly true for 
drugs used to treat serious conditions, where quick care with specific medications 
can mean the difference between life and death.  
 
Providers report that step therapy protocols frequently prioritize payer cost 
considerations over patient-specific clinical needs, forcing patients to cycle through 
therapies that are known to be less effective or inappropriate.15 Physician survey 
data indicate that step therapy requirements can delay initiation of prescribed 
therapy by weeks or longer, even when the treating clinician has identified the 
appropriate treatment upfront.16 
 
For patients with cancer, autoimmune conditions, rare diseases, and other serious 
illnesses, delays in starting effective therapy can result in disease progression, 
preventable complications, and deterioration in quality of life. 
 
 
While stronger interoperability is a step in the right direction to avoid delays, BIO 
urges CMS to take further action to ensure step therapy does not impede timely 
access to clinically appropriate care, particularly for patients with serious and 
life-threatening conditions. CMS should establish clear guardrails to ensure that any 
use of step therapy aligns with evidence-based clinical guidelines, respects physician 
judgment, and prioritizes patient health over other considerations.  
 
To further this end, BIO urges CMS to consider the following exceptions to fail-first 
step therapy:  
 
â€¢ 
When any treatments otherwise required under the protocol, or treatments in 
the same pharmacological class or having the same mechanism of action, 
have been ineffective in the treatment of the disease or condition of the 
participant or beneficiary, when prescribed consistent with clinical indications, 
clinical guidelines, or other peer-reviewed evidence. 
 
â€¢ 
When delay of effective treatment would lead to severe or irreversible 
consequences, and the treatment otherwise required under the protocol is 
reasonably expected to be ineffective based upon the documented physical or 
mental characteristics of the participant or beneficiary and the known 
characteristics of such treatment. 
 
â€¢ 
When any treatments otherwise required under the protocol are 
contraindicated for the participant or beneficiary or have caused, or are likely 
to cause, based on clinical, peer-reviewed evidence, an adverse reaction or 
other physical harm to the participant or beneficiary. 
 
â€¢ 
When any treatment otherwise required under the protocol has prevented, 
will prevent, or is likely to prevent a participant or beneficiary from achieving 
 
13 https://www.iqvia.com/-/media/iqvia/pdfs/us/white-paper/2025/iqvia-payer-controls-in-
part-d-white-paper-2025.pdf 
14 https://advisory.avalerehealth.com/insights/white-paper-provider-survey-on-part-b-step-
therapy-in-medicare-advantage 
15 https://www.ama-assn.org/system/files/prior-authorization-survey.pdf 
16 https://advisory.avalerehealth.com/insights/white-paper-provider-survey-on-part-b-step-
therapy-in-medicare-advantage 
13 
or maintaining reasonable and safe functional ability in performing 
occupational responsibilities or activities of daily living (as defined in section 
441.505 of title 42, Code of Federal Regulations (or successor regulations)). 
 
â€¢ 
When the participant or beneficiary is stable for his or her disease or condition 
on the prescription drug or drugs selected by the prescribing health care 
provider and has previously received approval for coverage of the relevant 
drug or drugs for the disease or condition by any group health plan or health 
insurance issuer. 
 
Finally, BIO encourages the Agency to recognize that plans may employ different 
utilization management approaches that are designed to achieve similar objectives, 
even if labeled differently. For example, both prior authorization and step therapy 
can create barriers to timely access to a provider-prescribed treatment. BIO 
recommends that the Agency consider these dynamics holistically and avoid 
situations where increased oversight of one form of utilization management 
inadvertently leads to greater use of other, functionally similar approaches. 
Taken together, BIO believes these criteria will help to ameliorate or eliminate 
harmful step therapy. 
 
Medicare Advantage Part B Drug Step Therapy Policy 
 
The Medicare Advantage Part B step therapy policy, often referred to as â€œfail first,â€ is 
harmful to patients. Implemented on January 1, 2019, this policy delays access to 
medically appropriate therapies, undermines physician judgment, and 
disproportionately harms patients with serious and complex conditions.17 BIO urges 
CMS to rescind the Part B Drug Step Therapy Policy. 
 
Treatment Abandonment and Downstream Utilization 
 
Importantly, similar to prior authorization, step therapy frequently leads to 
treatment abandonment. Patients who encounter repeated utilization management 
barriers, including step therapy followed by prior authorization, are substantially less 
likely to initiate any subsequent treatment, even when alternatives exist.18 
 
In these cases, utilization management is not effectively redirecting care or 
promoting appropriate therapy. It results in no care at all, increasing the risk of 
high-cost avoidable downstream utilization such as emergency department visits and 
hospitalizations. 
 
BIO urges CMS to collect data evaluating the frequency with which patients do not 
follow through with their care after being subject to step therapy.  
 
Application of Step Therapy to Medical Benefit Drugs 
 
BIO is particularly concerned that step therapy is increasingly applied to 
physician-administered drugs and therapies covered under the medical benefit, 
 
17 https://www.cms.gov/newsroom/fact-sheets/medicare-advantage-prior-authorization-
step-therapy-part-b-drugs 
18 https://www.iqvia.com/-/media/iqvia/pdfs/us/white-paper/2025/iqvia-payer-controls-in-
part-d-white-paper-2025.pdf 
14 
where clinical decision making is closely tied to disease severity, patient 
comorbidities, and treatment sequencing. 
 
Provider surveys demonstrate that step therapy protocols for medical-benefit drugs 
frequently interfere with physiciansâ€™ ability to deliver guideline-concordant care and 
are experienced by both providers and patients as highly burdensome.19  
 
Transparency, Data Availability, and Oversight of Step Therapy 
 
BIO encourages CMS to improve data transparency and public visibility around step 
therapy practices. At present, payer data concerning step therapy is largely opaque, 
limiting CMSâ€™s ability to evaluate how frequently step therapy is used, in what clinical 
contexts, and with what patient impact. 
 
Greater transparency would benefit patients, providers, and regulators alike. It 
would also aid in reducing the administrative burdens associated with appeals while 
mitigating risks to patient health. 
 
Regarding step therapy transparency and data collection, BIO urges CMS to: 
 
â€¢ 
Improve transparency around step therapy protocols, including greater 
public accessibility of utilization management criteria. While full 
proprietary criteria need not be disclosed, meaningful examples and 
clearer information would benefit patients and providers. This includes 
improving the transparency of step therapy that is embedded in prior 
authorizations to ensure that patients and providers have a clear 
understanding of coverage requirements 
 
â€¢ 
BIO urges CMS to require that regulated health plans annually report 
to CMS on step therapy activities, including which drugs, how often it 
is used, exception/appeal activity, and average timelines. This can be 
done in the manner that mirrors the prior authorization reporting 
proposed in the regulation.  
 
â€¢ 
Work with standards development organizations and stakeholders to 
define a core set of data elements and a consistent framework for 
tracking step therapy activity. Currently, there is no well-established 
minimum dataset or common terminology for step therapy. This limits 
both consistent measurement and seamless interoperability. BIO urges 
CMS to create a foundational set of data elements that includes when 
step therapy applies, what steps are required, whether a patient has 
already tried or failed a required therapy, whether exceptions are 
requested or granted, and whether step therapy determinations follow 
a patient across plan transitions. BIO believes that developing a 
standardized approach to these data elements would greatly improve 
transparency and support more consistent reporting. It would also 
align with CMS's broader interoperability goals and ensure patients 
undergoing step therapy have the most seamless experience.
 
19 https://advisory.avalerehealth.com/insights/white-paper-provider-survey-on-part-b-step-
therapy-in-medicare-advantage 
 
15 
 
â€¢ 
Use step therapy data collection to inform future CMS rulemaking, 
recognizing that better data is essential to assessing whether step therapy 
improves care or causes harm. 
 
Continuity of Care and Transitions Between Health Plans 
 
BIO further encourages CMS to ensure that step therapy requirements do not disrupt 
continuity of care when patients change health plans. Reducing duplicative step 
therapy during plan transitions would meaningfully improve patient experience and 
prevent unnecessary delays in care. 
 
CMS should leverage the payer-to-payer API finalized in the 2024 interoperability 
rule to ensure that patients transitioning between plans are not required to repeat 
step therapy requirements that have already been met. 
 
Timing and Implementation of Reforms 
 
CMSâ€™s interoperability efforts will not achieve their intended patient-centered goals if 
step therapy continues to operate as a structurally embedded barrier to care.  
 
BIO urges CMS to implement step therapy reforms as quickly as possible, 
recognizing that delays in implementing policy changes directly translate into delays 
in patient access to care. 
 
 
Conclusion 
 
BIO appreciates CMSâ€™s efforts to modernize prior authorization through interoperable, 
electronic processes and agrees that well-designed technology and processes have the 
potential to reduce administrative burden and improve patient experiences. 
 
However, for patients who rely on drugs to maintain their quality of life, the fundamental 
challenge remains the overuse and misapplication of utilization management. BIO urges 
CMS to ensure that implementation of CMS-0062-P meaningfully improves access to drugs, 
reduces unnecessary delays, and places patient health and outcomes at the center of prior 
authorization reform. 
 
BIO looks forward to continued engagement with CMS to advance policies that support 
timely access to medicines, promote innovation, and keep patients healthy. 
 
Sincerely,

# Comment Analysis Template: CMS-2026-1255-0001

## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** Biotechnology Innovation Organization (BIO); signed by Crystal Kuntz, Senior Vice President, Healthcare Policy & Reimbursement, and Luke Schwartz, Manager, Healthcare Policy & Reimbursement.
- **Stakeholder type:** Professional Association / Industry Association.
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** BIO represents biotechnology companies, industry leaders, and state biotech associations in the United States and more than 35 countries, including biopharmaceutical companies developing medicines.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

BIO supports standardized electronic prior authorization for drugs covered under both medical and pharmacy benefits, including FHIR-based APIs and NCPDP pharmacy standards, but warns that faster electronic workflows must not expand inappropriate utilization management. BIO recommends clinical guardrails, standardized PA data elements, continuity protections, near-real-time formulary/PA updates, stronger denial review and AI transparency, more frequent and granular PA reporting, narrowing the HIPAA direct data entry exception, and significant step therapy reforms including rescission of the Medicare Advantage Part B drug step therapy policy.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** FHIR-IG-REQUIRED; PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; PA-DENIAL-REASONS; PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS; API-USAGE-METRICS; HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS; GENERAL/RFI on step therapy.
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** Section 1927 of the Social Security Act; 42 CFR 441.505 referenced in step therapy exception criteria; CMS-0062-P; CMS-0057-F; 2024 Interoperability and Prior Authorization final rule; 2019 MA Part B step therapy policy.
- **Standards referenced:** FHIR; FHIR-based transactions; HIPAA transaction standards; direct data entry (DDE) exception; NCPDP SCRIPT, Formulary and Benefit, and Real-Time Prescription Benefit standards; Prior Authorization API; payer-to-payer API.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Standardized Interoperability APIs and FHIR Requirements**
- **Provision ID:** FHIR-IG-REQUIRED; HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS
- **Position:** Support / Modify
- **Rationale:** BIO agrees that standardized electronic exchange can reduce administrative burden, improve coordination, and support more accountable utilization management, but believes technology alone will not solve inappropriate PA or step therapy.
- **Specific request:** Finalize standardization while adding guardrails to ensure electronic PA improves patient access rather than merely accelerating denials or documentation requests.

**Topic 2: Electronic PA for Medical and Pharmacy Benefit Drugs**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Support / Modify
- **Rationale:** Fragmented manual workflows, payer-specific forms, duplicative documentation, and inconsistent coverage rules delay access to prescription drugs.
- **Specific request:** Require electronic PA capabilities for both medical and pharmacy benefit drugs, establish a standardized PA framework and common data elements all impacted payers must accept, and ensure PA is used only where clinically appropriate.

**Topic 3: Medical vs Pharmacy Benefit Pathway Assignment**
- **Provision ID:** MEDICAL-VS-PHARMACY-BENEFIT / PA-DRUG-MEDICAL / PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Clarify / Modify
- **Rationale:** Non-Medicare payer discretion to assign drugs to electronic PA pathways could cause avoidable delays or confusion without oversight.
- **Specific request:** CMS should monitor plan pathway determinations, create guardrails/reporting mechanisms, and require plans to redirect misrouted electronic PA requests to the correct pathway when required information is present.

**Topic 4: Formulary and PA Requirement Updates**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Patients and providers need current formulary and PA information, including mid-year changes, to avoid delays.
- **Specific request:** Require plans to update formulary and PA requirements in API portals as close to real time as possible.

**Topic 5: PA Decision Timeframes and Denial Communications**
- **Provision ID:** PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS; PA-DENIAL-REASONS
- **Position:** Support / Modify
- **Rationale:** Formal deadlines and specific denial reasons are necessary but insufficient if payers use repeated information requests, resubmissions, appeals, or AI tools to delay or deny clinically appropriate care.
- **Specific request:** Adopt and enforce proposed timelines, consider a uniform 24-hour timeline for urgent and non-urgent drug PA with oversight, require meaningful specific denial reasons, require clinician review/sign-off for AI-assisted adverse determinations, disclose AI involvement, and require specialist review of denials.

**Topic 6: Continuity of Care Across Payers**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Patients switching plans should not have to restart completed PA or step therapy processes.
- **Specific request:** Require payers to honor previous prescription drug PA approvals and leverage payer-to-payer APIs so step therapy determinations and exceptions follow patients across plan transitions.

**Topic 7: PA Metrics and Reporting**
- **Provision ID:** API-USAGE-METRICS
- **Position:** Support / Modify
- **Rationale:** Public metrics can identify excessive utilization management, inappropriate denials, delays, appeal reversals, and therapeutic areas with access problems.
- **Specific request:** Require public reporting of drug PA metrics, underlying counts, denials after appeal, extended-timeframe outcomes, therapeutic-area reporting, repeated denials, appeal reversals, and extended delays; allow CMS to require more frequent reporting when annual data show access concerns or outlier PA use.

**Topic 8: HIPAA Direct Data Entry Exception**
- **Provision ID:** HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Web portals remain burdensome and limit adoption of fully electronic standards-based transactions.
- **Specific request:** Narrow the DDE exception over time, retaining portals only as limited fallbacks rather than permanent substitutes for standards-based ePA.

**Topic 9: Step Therapy Reform**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL/RFI
- **Position:** Oppose / Modify
- **Rationale:** BIO argues step therapy can delay clinically appropriate therapy, interfere with physician judgment, worsen outcomes, and cause abandonment, especially for serious illnesses and medical benefit drugs.
- **Specific request:** Rescind the MA Part B drug step therapy policy, create evidence-based guardrails and exceptions, collect/report step therapy data, define standard data elements, improve transparency of protocols, and implement reforms quickly.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S1:** BIO supports stronger standardization of FHIR-based transactions and mandatory implementation consistency, while urging patient-centered guardrails.
- **S12:** BIO supports incorporating medical benefit drugs into the Prior Authorization API but asks CMS to ensure ePA does not increase inappropriate utilization management.
- **S14:** BIO supports applying NCPDP SCRIPT, Formulary and Benefit, and Real-Time Prescription Benefit standards to non-Medicare pharmacy benefit drugs.
- **S15:** BIO asks CMS to clarify oversight of payer drug-by-drug determinations of whether medical or pharmacy PA pathways apply and to require redirection of misrouted requests.
- **S16:** BIO supports requiring specific denial reasons and says denials must be meaningful, actionable, clinically appropriate, and transparent to patients and providers.
- **S17:** BIO does not focus on a specific code set but supports standardized data elements and clearer denial/step therapy reporting.
- **S20:** BIO supports 24-hour expedited drug PA timelines and statutory alignment for Medicaid covered outpatient drugs.
- **S21:** BIO supports the October 1, 2027 drug ePA framework but stresses that implementation must account for real-world provider workflows.
- **S22:** BIO does not quantify NCPDP costs but supports the pharmacy benefit standards because they can streamline ePA, formulary inquiries, and real-time benefit checks.
- **S25:** BIO supports real-time prescription benefit and formulary information and recommends near-real-time updates for formulary and PA requirements.
- **S28:** BIO supports alignment with Part D-like NCPDP standards for non-Medicare payers while preserving patient access safeguards.
- **S29:** BIO supports expanded PA metrics, including numerators/denominators, appeal outcomes, extended review outcomes, repeated denials, appeal reversals, extended delays, and therapeutic-area reporting.
- **S34:** BIO says annual reporting is insufficient in some cases and recommends CMS retain authority to trigger more frequent reporting for access concerns or outlier utilization management.
- **S35:** BIO supports public reporting but warns metrics must be interpreted in clinical context and not incentivize restrictive UM practices.
- **S44:** BIO supports FHIR standardization as a platform for improvement but emphasizes that standardization alone will not solve inappropriate utilization management.
- **S46:** BIO addresses coexistence with existing HIPAA workflows by urging CMS to narrow the DDE/web portal exception over time.
- **S47:** BIO acknowledges separate HIPAA compliance timing and supports moving away from web portals over time.
- **S50:** BIO treats FHIR-based standardization as sufficiently promising for PA improvement, while emphasizing guardrails and real-world monitoring.
- **S53:** BIO's recommendation to narrow DDE over time implies a phased transition toward standards-based electronic transactions.
- **S66-S82:** BIO responds extensively to the step therapy RFI, recommending data collection, continuity protections, exceptions, rescission of the MA Part B policy, and interoperability-supported transfer of step therapy history.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Finalize electronic PA requirements for drugs under both medical and pharmacy benefits.
2. Ensure ePA does not increase inappropriate, non-clinical, or overly complex utilization management.
3. Establish a standardized PA framework with common data elements, fields, and clinical questions that all impacted payers must accept.
4. Require payers to honor previous PA approvals for prescription drugs when patients switch coverage.
5. Monitor and evaluate payer decisions assigning drugs to medical or pharmacy ePA pathways.
6. Require plans to redirect misrouted PA requests to the proper pathway when all needed information is present.
7. Require near-real-time updates of formulary and PA requirements in API portals.
8. Consider a 24-hour timeline for both urgent and non-urgent drug PA decisions, with oversight to prevent rushed inappropriate denials.
9. Require clinician review and sign-off for AI-assisted denials or adverse PA determinations, disclose AI use, and explain the rationale.
10. Require denials to be reviewed by a specialist with expertise in the patient's diagnosis.
11. Collect public PA metrics with counts, appeal outcomes, extended-timeframe outcomes, repeated denials, appeal reversals, extended delays, and therapeutic-area breakouts.
12. Allow more frequent reporting when annual metrics show access concerns or PA use above benchmarks.
13. Narrow the HIPAA DDE/web portal exception over time.
14. Rescind the Medicare Advantage Part B drug step therapy policy.
15. Establish evidence-based step therapy guardrails, exceptions, data elements, reporting, and continuity protections.
16. Use payer-to-payer APIs so completed step therapy and exceptions follow patients across plan transitions.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** Overuse and misapplication of prior authorization and step therapy; technology-enabled faster denials; payer-specific PA requirements; care delays; low appeal rates despite high appeal success; insufficient annual reporting; DDE portal reliance; opaque step therapy practices.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Treatment abandonment, worsening symptoms, avoidable complications, emergency/inpatient utilization, disease progression, irreversible consequences for serious conditions, administrative burden on providers, and patient confusion.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** Fragmented workflows, manual processes, duplicative documentation, inconsistent coverage rules, payer-specific forms, misrouted medical/pharmacy pathway requests, mid-year formulary changes, AI opacity, web portals, and lack of step therapy data standards.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** KFF found PA ranked as the public's biggest healthcare burden; one-third of doctors have witnessed serious adverse events from excessive PA and untimely decisions; 93% of physicians reported PA caused care delays and 82% said it can lead to treatment abandonment; 80.7% of MA PA denials were eventually overturned on appeal while only 11.5% were appealed; providers and staff spend 13 hours per week on PA requests.
- **Studies or research referenced:** KFF polling and MA prior authorization analysis; National Organization for Rare Disorders survey; AMA prior authorization survey; IQVIA payer controls white paper; PAN Foundation State of Patient Access Report; Avalere/Advisory provider survey on Part B step therapy; CMS MA Part B step therapy policy documents.
- **Examples provided:** Rare disease patients, cancer, autoimmune disease, rare genetic disorders, medical benefit drugs, fail-first step therapy, patients stable on current therapies, and patients changing health plans.

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** Patients needing prescription drugs, rare disease patients, biopharmaceutical innovators, prescribers, providers and staff, MA organizations, Medicaid/CHIP payers, QHP issuers, CMS, standards development organizations, and health plans using PA/step therapy tools.
- **Economic implications:** Standardized ePA can reduce administrative burden and duplicative data entry, but restrictive UM can cause downstream emergency/inpatient utilization and treatment abandonment. Reporting and oversight require payer and CMS investment but may improve accountability.
- **Technical feasibility:** BIO supports FHIR and NCPDP-based infrastructure as feasible but stresses the need for standardized data elements, near-real-time updates, pathway monitoring, and transition away from DDE portals.
- **Patient care impact:** High. BIO argues the rule could improve access if paired with guardrails, but could worsen access if it simply makes denials and UM more efficient.

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Mixed: supportive of interoperability/ePA standardization, strongly concerned about utilization management abuse.
- **Tone:** Professional, evidence-based, and critical.
- **Priority level:** High.

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "BIO supports CMS's proposal to require electronic prior authorization capabilities for prescription drugs." - Context: Core support for drug ePA expansion.
2. "Faster denials or more efficient requests for additional documentation do not constitute meaningful reform from a patient perspective." - Context: Warning that ePA must improve access, not just process speed.
3. "BIO encourages CMS to narrow the direct data entry exception over time." - Context: HIPAA/DDE recommendation.
4. "BIO urges CMS to rescind the Part B Drug Step Therapy Policy." - Context: Step therapy RFI recommendation.

## 12. THEMES

- [x] **IMPLEMENTATION-TIMELINE** - BIO addresses October 1, 2027 implementation, decision deadlines, more frequent reporting, and rapid step therapy reforms.
- [x] **COST-RESOURCES** - The comment cites provider staff time, administrative burden, and downstream emergency/inpatient utilization.
- [x] **PROVIDER-BURDEN** - Provider workflow burden from forms, portals, duplicative documentation, and payer-specific fields is a major focus.
- [x] **TECHNICAL-FEASIBILITY** - BIO discusses FHIR, NCPDP, DDE portals, standardized data elements, real-time updates, AI tools, and payer-to-payer APIs.
- [x] **STANDARDS-MATURITY** - The comment supports standardizing ePA transactions but asks for more mature common data elements and step therapy data standards.
- [x] **PATIENT-ACCESS** - Timely access to clinically appropriate prescription medicines is BIO's central concern.
- [x] **TRANSPARENCY** - BIO requests transparent denial reasons, AI disclosure, PA metrics, step therapy protocols, and public reporting.
- [x] **STAKEHOLDER-COORDINATION** - The comment calls for CMS, plans, SDOs, providers, and stakeholders to coordinate on data elements, reporting, and policy safeguards.
- [x] **MEDICAL-VS-PHARMACY-BENEFIT** - BIO asks CMS to monitor and clarify drug pathway assignments and misrouted requests.
- [x] **EXISTING-WORKFLOWS** - The comment addresses web portals, provider PA workflows, appeals, step therapy, plan transitions, and formulary updates.
- [x] **VENDOR-ECOSYSTEM** - AI-based PA tools, API portals, and standards-based transaction vendors are implicated by BIO's recommendations.
